attempts.why: To verify the company's cash balances throughout the year and confirm they agree with the bank's records, we need to see each account's activity and balances.
attempts.good_looks_like: A bank statement for every account the company held during the year, covering each month of the period. Each statement should show the opening balance, transactions, and closing balance. Download them as PDFs from online banking; photos or scans are harder to read.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need bank statements (verify cash balances and confirm agreement with bank records), describes exactly what a complete document looks like (monthly statements for all accounts with opening/closing balances and transactions), uses plain language throughout, and avoids audit jargon entirely. The practical guidance about PDFs vs. scans is helpful.
attempts.description: Bank statements for all accounts, every month of the period

attempts.why: To confirm the cash the company held throughout the year and verify all bank account activity agrees with your accounting records.
attempts.good_looks_like: A bank statement for every account the company held during the year, covering each month from the start of the period to the year-end date. Download statements as PDFs from online banking; scans or photos are harder to read. Include statements even for accounts closed during the year.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need bank statements (to confirm cash held and verify activity matches records), describes exactly what a complete document set looks like (monthly statements for all accounts including closed ones, in PDF format), uses plain language throughout, and contains no unexplained jargon.
attempts.description: Bank statements for all accounts, every month of the period

attempts.why: To confirm that the company's cash balance in the accounting system matches what the bank records show at year end, and to explain any differences.
attempts.good_looks_like: A bank reconciliation for each account as of the year-end date, showing the bank's closing balance, the accounting system balance, and a line-by-line list of items that explain the difference (such as cheques not yet cleared or deposits not yet processed). The total should agree with your accounting system.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need bank reconciliations (to verify cash balances match and explain differences). It describes a complete document with all required elements: bank balance, accounting balance, line-by-line differences, and agreement check. Language is accessible to non-accountants. Minor: 'cheques not yet cleared' and 'deposits not yet processed' are common terms but could be slightly simpler (e.g., 'checks the bank hasn't processed yet').

attempts.why: To confirm the cash the company held at year end, we compare each bank account's balance with the bank's own record.
attempts.good_looks_like: A bank confirmation letter from each bank where the company holds an account, dated at or shortly after the year-end date. The letter should come directly from the bank on its letterhead and show the account number, the balance at year end, and any authorized signatories. If the bank won't send a letter, a bank statement for each account covering the year-end date with opening and closing balances will work instead.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why (verify cash balances against bank records) and describes acceptable documents in detail (confirmation letter with specific elements, or bank statement alternative). Language is accessible to non-accountants. Minor: 'authorized signatories' is mildly technical but contextually clear.

attempts.why: To confirm the petty cash the company held at year end matches your accounting records and that the cash physically exists.
attempts.good_looks_like: A record of the petty cash count performed at or very close to the year-end date, showing the amount counted, who counted it, the date and time of the count, and confirmation it agrees with your accounting system.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why the auditor needs the petty cash count (to verify existence and accuracy), describes what a complete document includes (amount, who counted, date/time, agreement with records), uses straightforward language accessible to non-accountants, and avoids audit jargon entirely.

attempts.why: To see who owes the company money at year end and for how long, and to check it agrees with your accounting system.
attempts.good_looks_like: An aged receivables report as of the year-end date, by customer, with totals by age band (for example, current, 30 days overdue, 60 days overdue, 90+ days overdue), exported from your accounting system without edits.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why the auditor needs the document (to verify who owes money and reconcile to the system), describes a complete acceptable format with specific details (by customer, age bands, year-end date, unedited export), and uses plain language. Minor deduction for 'aged receivables report' and 'age band' which, while common, could be briefly explained for a non-accountant.
attempts.description: Accounts receivable aging at period end

attempts.why: To confirm that amounts customers owed at year end were genuine, we check whether the company received payment after year end.
attempts.good_looks_like: A report or spreadsheet showing amounts received from customers in the period after the year-end date, matched to invoices or customer accounts from year end. Include the customer name, invoice date, amount received, and date of receipt.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains the audit purpose (confirming year-end receivables were real by checking post-year-end payments). The 'good_looks_like' section is specific and complete, covering format, content, and matching requirements. Language is accessible to non-accountants. Minor: 'subsequent receipts testing' in the request title is audit jargon, but the draft itself avoids it and explains the concept plainly.

attempts.why: To verify the allowance for doubtful accounts is calculated correctly and supported by evidence of which receivables may not be collected.
attempts.good_looks_like: A spreadsheet showing how the allowance was calculated at the year-end date. Include the method used (such as a percentage of sales, aging analysis, or individual customer assessment), the receivables or customer balances it applies to, and the resulting allowance amount. The total should agree with your accounting system.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why the auditor needs this (to verify calculation and identify uncollectible receivables). The 'good_looks_like' section is thorough, covering method, scope, amount, and reconciliation. Language is mostly accessible, but 'allowance for doubtful accounts' and 'aging analysis' are accounting terms that could confuse non-accountants, though the context provides some clarity.

attempts.why: To see what the company owed its suppliers at year end and confirm nothing is missing.
attempts.good_looks_like: An aged payables report as of the year-end date, by supplier, with totals by age band, exported from your accounting system without edits.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains the business purpose (what company owed, completeness check) in accessible language. The 'good_looks_like' section is specific and complete. Minor deduction for 'aged payables' and 'age band' which are accounting terms, though context makes them understandable.
attempts.description: Accounts payable aging at period end

attempts.why: To check that all amounts the company owed at year end are recorded in the accounts, we need to see the evidence you used to search for any liabilities that might have been missed.
attempts.good_looks_like: Documentation of your search for unrecorded liabilities, such as: a list of suppliers contacted after year end to confirm amounts owed; bank statements and credit card statements for the period after year end showing payments made; correspondence with creditors; or a summary of procedures performed to identify any invoices received after year end for goods or services provided before year end. Include dates and amounts where relevant.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why (to verify all debts are recorded) and describes complete acceptable evidence with specific examples and details. Language is mostly accessible but uses 'liabilities' and 'unrecorded' which, while standard accounting terms, could be briefly explained for non-accountants. The term 'year end' is used without definition.

attempts.why: To check that all amounts the company owed at year end are recorded in the accounts, we need to see the evidence you used to search for any liabilities that might have been missed.
attempts.good_looks_like: Documentation of your search for unrecorded liabilities, such as: a list of suppliers contacted after year end to confirm amounts owed; bank statements and credit card statements for the period after year end showing payments made; correspondence with creditors; or a summary of procedures performed to identify any invoices received after year end for goods or services provided before year end. Include dates and amounts where relevant.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why (to verify all debts are recorded) and describes complete acceptable evidence with specific examples and details. Language is mostly accessible but uses 'liabilities' and 'unrecorded' which, while standard accounting terms, could be briefly explained for non-accountants. The term 'year end' is used without definition.

attempts.why: To see what costs the company has incurred but not yet paid at year end, and to confirm the accrual is complete and accurate.
attempts.good_looks_like: A spreadsheet listing each accrued expense item at the year-end date, with descriptions, amounts, and the total that agrees with your accounting system. Include the supplier or cost category for each item.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need accrued expenses (to verify costs incurred but unpaid) in plain language. The 'good_looks_like' section is specific and practical. Minor deduction for 'accrual' and 'accounting system' which could be briefly explained for non-accountants, though context makes them understandable.

attempts.why: To verify the inventory quantities the company recorded at year end, we need to see how the physical count was performed and what was found.
attempts.good_looks_like: Documentation of the inventory count process, including the date(s) it took place, the locations counted, the method used (such as full count or cycle count), and the results showing quantities by item or location. This should tie to the inventory balance in your accounting system at year end. Provide count sheets, reconciliations, or a summary report in spreadsheet or document form.
attempts.judge_note: The 'why' clearly explains the auditor needs to verify recorded quantities match physical reality. The 'good_looks_like' is thorough and specific about what documents are needed. Language is accessible, though 'cycle count' and 'reconciliations' could be briefly explained for non-accountants. Overall well-written and client-friendly.

attempts.why: To confirm how the company values its inventory at year end and that the cost is accurate, we need to understand the methods used and see the calculations behind the reported balance.
attempts.good_looks_like: A summary of the inventory valuation methods used (such as first-in-first-out, weighted average, or standard cost), any adjustments made at year end (for obsolescence, damage or slow-moving stock), and a spreadsheet showing how the final inventory balance was calculated and agreed to the accounting system.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need this (to confirm valuation methods and accuracy). The 'good_looks_like' section is comprehensive, covering methods, adjustments, and calculations. Language is mostly accessible, though 'obsolescence' and 'weighted average' may need brief explanation for non-accountants. Some audit terminology present ('year end', 'accounting system', 'balance') but generally understandable in context.

attempts.why: To see how the company's property and equipment balance changed during the year, including additions, disposals, and depreciation, and to confirm it agrees with your accounting system.
attempts.good_looks_like: A spreadsheet showing each asset or asset category with its opening balance at the start of the year, additions and disposals during the year, depreciation charged, and closing balance at the year-end date. Include a total row that agrees with your accounting system.
attempts.judge_note: The 'why' clearly explains the auditor's need to verify asset changes and system agreement. The 'good_looks_like' is comprehensive and specific about required components and totals. Language is mostly accessible but 'disposals,' 'depreciation,' and 'rollforward' (implied in context) may need brief explanation for non-accountant clients. 'Depreciation charged' is the main jargon term not explained.

attempts.why: To verify that fixed asset additions recorded in your accounts are genuine, properly valued, and correctly classified.
attempts.good_looks_like: Copies of invoices for all fixed asset purchases above your capitalization threshold during the year, showing the vendor, description of the asset, purchase date, and amount. Invoices should be in their original form (PDF or scanned) and cover the full year.
attempts.judge_note: The 'why' clearly explains the audit purpose (verify genuineness, valuation, classification). The 'good_looks_like' is thorough and specific about what's needed. Language is mostly plain but 'capitalization threshold' and 'classified' may confuse non-accountants. 'Fixed asset' is standard but could be explained as 'equipment or property you own'.
attempts.description: Invoices for fixed asset additions over the threshold

attempts.why: To verify that depreciation expense for the year is calculated correctly and that accumulated depreciation on the balance sheet is accurate.
attempts.good_looks_like: A spreadsheet showing each asset or asset category, its cost, useful life in years, depreciation method (such as straight-line), opening accumulated depreciation, depreciation charged for the year, and closing accumulated depreciation as of the year-end date. The total closing accumulated depreciation should agree with your accounting system.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need the schedule (verify calculations and balance sheet accuracy). The 'good_looks_like' section comprehensively describes required elements with proper date/period coverage. Language is mostly accessible but uses accounting terms like 'accumulated depreciation,' 'straight-line,' and 'balance sheet' without explanation, which a non-accountant might not fully understand. Some jargon ('useful life,' 'depreciation method') appears without definition.

attempts.why: To understand the terms of the company's debt, including interest rates, repayment schedules and any covenants, and to confirm the year-end balance is complete and accurate.
attempts.good_looks_like: Copies of all debt agreements in place at year end, including loan agreements, credit facilities and any bonds or notes issued. Include any amendments or side letters signed during the year that change the original terms. Provide the documents as they were signed, or as updated if formally amended.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need debt agreements (to verify terms, rates, schedules, covenants, and year-end completeness). The 'good_looks_like' section is comprehensive, specifying document types, timing, and format. Language is mostly plain; 'covenants' is technical but contextually clear. Minor: 'side letters' and 'formally amended' are slightly specialized but understandable to most business owners.

attempts.why: To understand the terms of the company's debt, including interest rates, repayment schedules and any covenants, and to confirm the year-end balance is complete and accurate.
attempts.good_looks_like: Copies of all debt agreements in place at year end, including loan agreements, credit facilities and any bonds or notes issued. Include any amendments or side letters signed during the year that change the original terms. Provide the documents as they were signed, or as updated if formally amended.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need debt agreements (to verify terms, rates, schedules, covenants, and year-end completeness). The 'good_looks_like' section is comprehensive, specifying document types, timing, and format. Language is mostly plain; 'covenants' is technical but contextually clear. Minor: 'side letters' and 'formally amended' are slightly specialized but understandable to most business owners.

attempts.why: To verify the company complied with its debt covenants at year end and understand any waivers or breaches that may affect the financial statements.
attempts.good_looks_like: A spreadsheet or document showing each debt covenant, the calculation method, the actual result at the year-end date, the required threshold, and whether it was met. Include the source of each figure (such as the accounting system or loan agreement) and any covenant waivers or amendments signed during the year.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need covenant compliance data (to verify compliance and identify breaches affecting financials). The 'good_looks_like' section is thorough and specific about required content, calculations, thresholds, sources, and waivers. Language is mostly accessible but uses terms like 'covenant,' 'threshold,' and 'waivers' without explanation—a non-accountant client might need clarification on these audit-specific concepts.

attempts.why: To verify that interest expense recorded in the year is accurate and complete, we recalculate it from the underlying debt agreements and balances.
attempts.good_looks_like: A spreadsheet showing each debt facility held during the year, with the interest rate, opening and closing balances, and the interest expense calculated for the year. Include a total that agrees with the interest expense in your accounting system at year end.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains the audit purpose (verify accuracy and completeness of interest expense). 'Good_looks_like' is specific and complete, covering all needed elements (facilities, rates, balances, calculations, totals, reconciliation). Language is accessible to non-accountants. Minor jargon: 'debt facilities' and 'interest expense' are standard business terms that most clients understand, though 'recalculate from underlying debt agreements' could be slightly simpler.

attempts.why: To understand the company's ownership structure at year end and verify that share issuances, repurchases, and transfers are recorded correctly in the accounting system.
attempts.good_looks_like: A spreadsheet or document showing each shareholder's name, number of shares held, share class, and percentage ownership as of the year-end date. Include a summary of all share transactions during the year (issuances, repurchases, transfers) with dates and quantities. The total shares outstanding should agree with your accounting system.
attempts.judge_note: Explains why clearly (verify ownership and transactions). Describes complete document well (names, shares, classes, dates, totals). Uses some accounting terms ('share class,' 'accounting system') without explanation. Could simplify for non-accountant.

attempts.why: To confirm that any dividends paid or declared during the year were properly authorized by the board before payment or announcement.
attempts.good_looks_like: Board minutes or resolutions from board meetings held during the year that document approval of dividends, including the date approved, amount per share, and payment date. If dividends were declared after year end but relate to the year, include those approvals too.
attempts.judge_note: Clearly explains auditors need board approval documentation to verify dividends were authorized. Describes complete acceptable documents with specific details (date, amount per share, payment date). Language is accessible; 'declared after year end' is the only slightly technical phrase but is explained in context.

attempts.why: To understand the terms of your significant customer contracts and confirm revenue is recognized correctly and completely at year end.
attempts.good_looks_like: Copies of the signed contracts for each significant customer, showing the key terms: what goods or services are provided, the price, payment terms, and any conditions that affect when revenue should be recognized (such as performance milestones or return rights). If contracts are very long, a summary of these key points is acceptable.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need contracts (to verify revenue recognition is correct and complete). 'Good looks like' is thorough and practical, covering key terms, dates, and offering a summary alternative for lengthy documents. Language is accessible to non-accountants. Minor: 'revenue is recognized' uses accounting terminology, though the context makes it understandable.

attempts.why: To confirm that sales are recorded in the correct period, we test transactions around the year-end date to ensure revenue is recognized when goods or services are delivered, not when the invoice is sent or payment is received.
attempts.good_looks_like: A list of sales transactions from a few days before and after the year-end date, showing the invoice date, delivery date, and amount for each. Include enough detail to let us trace each transaction back to your accounting system and supporting documents like delivery notes or customer confirmations.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why (cutoff testing ensures correct period recording) and describes a complete, traceable document set with specific details (invoice date, delivery date, amounts, supporting docs). Language is mostly accessible but uses terms like 'revenue is recognized' and 'cutoff' without explanation, which a non-accountant may not fully understand. Otherwise well-structured and practical.

attempts.why: To understand how deferred revenue changed during the year and confirm the year-end balance is accurate and complete.
attempts.good_looks_like: A spreadsheet showing deferred revenue by type or contract, with opening balance at the start of the year, amounts received or recognized during the year, and closing balance at the year-end date. The closing balance should agree with your accounting system.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why (verify accuracy and completeness of year-end balance) and describes a complete rollforward with opening/closing balances and reconciliation. Language is accessible to non-accountants. Minor issue: 'deferred revenue' and 'accounting system' are accounting terms not explained, though 'deferred revenue' is the document's subject so some use is unavoidable.

attempts.why: To verify the payroll costs recorded in your accounts and check that employee deductions and employer contributions are correct.
attempts.good_looks_like: The payroll register for each of the two pay periods, showing gross pay, all deductions (tax, social security, pension, etc.), net pay, and employer contributions by employee. Export directly from your payroll system without edits, and confirm the totals agree with your accounting records for those periods.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why (verify costs and check deductions/contributions) and gives precise, actionable guidance on what a complete document looks like. Language is mostly accessible, but 'employer contributions' and 'deductions' could be briefly explained for a non-accounting client. No audit jargon is used, though the explanation assumes some payroll familiarity.
attempts.description: Payroll registers for two pay periods

attempts.why: To verify the payroll taxes the company reported and paid to tax authorities during the year, and to check they agree with your payroll records.
attempts.good_looks_like: Copies of all quarterly payroll tax returns filed for the year, as submitted to the relevant tax authority. Include the filing confirmation or receipt showing the date filed and any reference number.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need the documents (verify reported/paid taxes and reconcile with records). The 'good_looks_like' section is specific and complete (all quarterly returns, filing confirmations, dates, reference numbers). Language is plain and accessible. Minor: 'payroll tax returns' and 'tax authority' are standard terms most business owners understand, but could be slightly more conversational.

attempts.why: To verify that bonuses owed to employees at year end are complete and accurate, and that the accrual in your accounts is correct.
attempts.good_looks_like: A spreadsheet or document showing how the bonus accrual was calculated at the year-end date: the employees eligible, the bonus amount or formula for each, and the total accrued. It should tie to your payroll records and accounting system.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why (verify completeness and accuracy of bonus obligations), describes what a complete document looks like with specific details (employees, amounts, totals, ties to records), and uses plain language. Minor deduction for 'accrual' and 'tie' which are slightly technical but contextually clear.

attempts.why: To identify all leases the company is party to and understand their key terms, we need to review the agreements themselves.
attempts.good_looks_like: Copies of all lease agreements in effect at the year-end date or signed during the year, including any amendments or side letters. Include leases for property, equipment, vehicles or other assets, whether the company is the lessee or lessor. Provide them as PDFs or scans, ideally organized by asset type or lease commencement date.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need leases (to identify agreements and understand terms). The 'good_looks_like' section is thorough, covering scope (all leases, amendments), parties (lessee/lessor), asset types, timing, and format. Language is accessible to non-accountants. Minor: 'year-end date' could be slightly simpler, but is standard business terminology. No audit jargon present.

attempts.why: To see what leases the company has, their key terms, and how the lease liability and right-of-use asset are calculated at year end.
attempts.good_looks_like: A spreadsheet listing each lease, with columns for the lease term, commencement date, payment amounts, discount rate used, and the resulting lease liability and right-of-use asset balance as of the year-end date. Include a total row that agrees with your accounting system.
attempts.judge_note: The 'why' clearly explains the auditor's need to verify lease accounting. The 'good_looks_like' is detailed and complete. Language is mostly accessible but uses accounting terms ('lease liability,' 'right-of-use asset,' 'discount rate') without explanation, which a non-accountant client may not understand. These terms should be briefly defined or contextualized.
attempts.description: Lease liability and right-of-use asset schedule

attempts.why: To identify any legal claims, disputes or obligations the company faces that may need to be recorded or disclosed in the financial statements.
attempts.good_looks_like: A letter from each law firm or legal advisor the company uses, dated at or shortly after the year-end date, confirming the status of any pending or threatened litigation, claims, or legal matters. The letter should describe each matter, its likely outcome, and any estimated financial exposure. If there are no matters, the letter should confirm that too.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need legal letters (to identify claims affecting financial statements). The 'good_looks_like' section is thorough and specific about what constitutes a complete letter. Language is mostly accessible, though 'financial exposure' and 'contingencies' are accounting terms that could be briefly explained for a non-accountant. Overall, a strong draft with minor room for simplification.

attempts.why: To verify the insurance policies the company has in place at year end and confirm the prepaid insurance balance is accurate and supported.
attempts.good_looks_like: Copies of all active insurance policies and certificates as of the year-end date, showing the policyholder, coverage type, coverage period, premium amount, and renewal date. Include any endorsements or amendments. Provide them as PDFs or scans, organized by policy type.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why (verify policies and support prepaid balance). The 'good_looks_like' is thorough and specific about what to provide. Language is mostly accessible, though 'policyholder,' 'endorsements,' and 'prepaid insurance balance' might need brief explanation for non-accounting clients. 'Prepaid insurance balance' is audit-specific jargon that could be simplified to 'the amount we show on the balance sheet for insurance paid in advance.'

attempts.why: To see what prepaid expenses the company has at year end and confirm the total agrees with your accounting system.
attempts.good_looks_like: A spreadsheet listing each prepaid expense item at the year-end date—such as insurance, subscriptions, or rent paid in advance—with the amount for each, and a total that matches your accounting system. Include the date each was paid and when it expires or is used up.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need prepaid expenses (to verify what exists and reconcile to records). The 'good_looks_like' section is thorough, specifying format, content, dates, and reconciliation requirement. Language is accessible to non-accountants throughout. No unexplained jargon; 'prepaid expenses' is the standard term but is self-explanatory in context. Minor: could slightly strengthen 'why' by mentioning accuracy of financial statements, but current explanation is solid.

attempts.why: To verify the income tax provision recorded in your financial statements is complete and accurate, and to confirm the underlying calculations and assumptions.
attempts.good_looks_like: A workpaper or set of documents showing how the income tax provision was calculated at year end. This should include: the taxable income or loss, the applicable tax rate(s), any adjustments or timing differences, deferred tax calculations if relevant, and a summary showing how the final provision amount was determined. The total should agree with what's in your accounting system.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why (verify accuracy and completeness) and provides detailed, specific guidance on what constitutes an acceptable document. Language is mostly accessible, though terms like 'provision,' 'deferred tax,' and 'timing differences' may need brief explanation for non-accountant clients. The 'complete' section is thorough and well-structured.

attempts.why: To understand the company's tax position in prior years and identify any open issues or adjustments that may affect the current year.
attempts.good_looks_like: Copies of the company's filed tax returns for the prior two years, as submitted to the tax authority. Include all schedules, attachments and any correspondence from the tax authority regarding assessments or adjustments.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why tax returns are needed (understand tax position, identify open issues). The 'good_looks_like' section is thorough and specific about what documents to provide. Language is mostly accessible, though 'tax authority,' 'assessments,' and 'adjustments' may need brief explanation for non-accountant clients. The term 'tax position' is slightly technical but contextually clear.

attempts.why: To understand the company's governance, key decisions made during the year, and any significant events after year end that may affect the financial statements.
attempts.good_looks_like: Copies of all board meeting minutes for the year, and any minutes or records of meetings held after the year-end date up to the date the financial statements are approved. Minutes should show the date, attendees, and decisions made.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why auditors need board minutes (understanding governance and decisions), provides a complete description of what's needed (all minutes for the year plus post-year-end through approval, with specific content details), and uses plain language. The term 'subsequent events' in the why section is mild audit jargon, but the explanation makes it clear enough. Overall, this is a well-written client request.
attempts.description: Board minutes for the period and subsequent events

attempts.why: To identify all transactions between the company and related parties at year end, and to check they are properly disclosed and recorded at the correct amounts.
attempts.good_looks_like: A spreadsheet listing each related party transaction for the year, with the related party's name or description, the nature of the transaction, the amount, and the accounting treatment. Include a total that agrees with your accounting system. Related parties include owners, directors, key management, and entities they control.
attempts.judge_note: The 'why' clearly explains the audit purpose (identify transactions, verify disclosure and recording). The 'good_looks_like' is comprehensive and specific (spreadsheet format, required fields, reconciliation to accounting system). Language is mostly accessible but uses 'related parties,' 'accounting treatment,' and 'disclosure' without explanation—terms a non-accountant may not fully understand. Overall strong, with minor jargon clarity needed.

attempts.why: We need written confirmation from management that all material facts about the company's finances and operations have been disclosed to us, and that the financial statements are complete and accurate.
attempts.good_looks_like: A letter on company letterhead, signed by an authorized member of management (usually the chief executive or finance director), confirming that they have disclosed all relevant information to the auditor, that the financial statements are fairly presented, and that there are no undisclosed liabilities, fraud, or legal disputes.
attempts.judge_note: The 'why' clearly explains the auditor's need for management confirmation. The 'good_looks_like' is thorough and specific about format, signatory, and content. However, 'plain' is reduced because phrases like 'material facts' and 'fairly presented' may confuse non-accountants. 'No_jargon' is lower due to terms like 'disclosed,' 'liabilities,' and 'material' without explanation—a client might not understand why these specific items matter or what 'material' means in this context.

attempts.why: To confirm the balances in your accounting system at year end and ensure they're complete and accurate, we compare them with your trial balance.
attempts.good_looks_like: Your trial balance as of the year-end date, listing every account with its debit or credit balance, exported directly from your accounting system without edits. The total debits must equal total credits.
attempts.judge_note: The draft clearly explains why (verification of year-end balances) and describes a complete document well. Language is mostly accessible, but 'trial balance,' 'debit,' 'credit,' and 'accounting system' are accounting terms not explained for a non-accountant. The phrase 'without edits' is clear and helpful.

attempts.why: To understand all the manual entries the company recorded in its accounting system during the year, we need a complete list of them.
attempts.good_looks_like: A report from your accounting system listing every manual journal entry recorded for the year, with columns showing the date, description, accounts affected, and amounts debited and credited. Export it without filtering or editing, and include entries from all periods.
attempts.judge_note: The 'why' states what is needed but doesn't explain the audit purpose (e.g., detecting errors, unauthorized transactions, or account reconciliation). The 'good_looks_like' is clear and specific about format and scope.
